newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk minister says no Kurd problem, only terror.
newsitem.headline: Turk minister says no Kurd problem, only terror.

text.p: Turkey, faced with a European legal assault on its treatment of the Kurds, said on Wednesday that Western critics ignored the fact that security forces were engaged in a tough fight with Kurdish separatist guerrillas.
"There is no Kurdish problem in Turkey, but a terror problem. It is the West which calls it the Kurdish problem to divide Turkey," Justice Minister Sevket Kazan told reporters.
His ministry is to take on the task of defending Ankara in 61 cases against Turkey in the European Court of Human Rights stemming from alleged human rights abuses in the mainly Kurdish southeast.

Fighting between Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) guerrillas and government forces has cost 21,000 lives in the last 12 years. Successive governments have refused to consider demands for Kurdish self-rule.
Kazan said Turkey would scrap the state security courts, powerful judicial instruments often used to crack down on Kurdish and far-left dissent, as part of human rights reforms.
"We will abolish the state security courts in two years at the latest...The state security courts, which include a military judge, are not natural and felony courts can fulfil their duties," he said.
Kazan said around 9,200 people were on trial or waiting to be tried at the security courts, a residue from the 1980-82 military rule era.
Leaders of Turkey's only legal Kurdish party are facing up to 22 1/2 years in jail for separatism in a security court trial after a pro-PKK demonstration at a party congress in June.
The European Court cases are only part of the foreign human rights pressure on Turkey.
Amnesty International launched a worldwide campaign against Turkey in October, focusing on extra-judical killings, disappearances and torture.
The European Parliament, angered by Turkey's rights record, has voted to suspend hundreds of millions of dollars of aid planned to help Ankara set up a customs union with the European Union.
Kazan said Turkey would put its case vigorously at the European Court despite the recent resignation of the lawyer who had been defending Turkey.
The lawyer quit his post in late October, complaining that his country had failed to fulfil promises to improve its rights performance.
Kazan complained that the court had broken its own rules by taking on the cases before they had gone through the ponderous Turkish legal system.

"The court accepted some of the applications against Turkey without exhausting domestic legal channels first and some of the applications are controversial. The court must fulfil its own rules," he said.
The rights problem has also hindered Turkey's planned entry into the EU but President Suleyman Demirel said on Wednesday it was only a matter of time before Turkey became a full member.
"Membership of the European Union is our priority," he told reporters after meeting Germany Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
He was on the second day of a state visit to Germany that has been dogged by Kurdish demonstrations and human rights protests.
